web_evidence.title: Lincoln: American Chronicle Series
web_evidence.note: The licensed ebook preview supplies a sustained opening narrated externally around Washburne, including access to his temper, caution, wishes, and perceptions, all in third person.

web_evidence.title: Backlash Realism: The American Novel during the Long 1980s
web_evidence.note: Seth Studer's Tufts dissertation analyzes Lincoln's complete narrative structure as omniscient narration with free-indirect discourse and explicitly identifies direct third-person passages and six principal third-person focal perspectives.

web_evidence.title: Gore Vidal's 'Lincoln'?: An Exchange
web_evidence.note: Vidal explains his Jamesian method: scenes are observed through individual characters' consciousnesses, while Lincoln is shown through those around him rather than by a participating narrator or Lincoln's own narration.

web_evidence.title: Gore Vidal Writing Styles in Lincoln
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly describes the novel as third-person, past-tense narration that shifts among characters' points of view.

person_note: The diagnostic quotes repeatedly use external third-person narration with access to Seward's, Hay's, Chase's, Booth's, and Washburne's private perceptions. First- and second-person forms elsewhere are local dialogue, not narrator participation. The sustained opening independently agrees, and the Tufts whole-book analysis confirms that the shifting consciousnesses and occasional direct narration remain third person. Vidal's own account and the explicit study-guide description corroborate this structure. Multiple focal characters therefore do not constitute person alternation. The quote set is dialogue-heavy and the Tier A prose covers only the opening, but the whole-book scholarly evidence resolves that coverage limitation, and no credible contrary structure was found.
